statement: A clock with hands but no numbers hangs opposite a mirror. In the mirror, the clock seems to show exactly 4 o'clock. What time is it really?

choices.misconception: I flipped the clock top to bottom instead of left to right.
I thought a mirror shows the time without changing it.
I counted back 4 from 12 but counted the 12 itself as the first step.
I turned the clock upside down, which moves each hand to the opposite side.

hints: A mirror swaps left and right, but keeps the 12 at the top.
Picture the hour hand being reflected in the line from 12 to 6. A hand that is some hours past 12 on one side ends up the same number of hours before 12 on the other.
In the mirror the hour hand is 4 hours clockwise from 12. On the real clock it is 4 hours anticlockwise from 12.

solutions.reliable: The mirror swaps left and right, so the line from 12 to 6 stays put and everything else flips across it. The minute hand stays on 12. An hour hand 4 hours clockwise from 12 in the mirror is really 4 hours anticlockwise from 12, which is 8. So it is really 8 o'clock. The transferable idea: a left-right reflection sends hour h to 12 - h.
solutions.elegant: Mirror time and real time always add up to 12 hours on the hour: 4 + 8 = 12. Check with an easy case: at 6 o'clock the hand points straight down and looks the same in a mirror, and 6 + 6 = 12. The transferable idea: test a rule on a case you can see.

whyOnTest: Reflections on a clock face: knowing which line stays fixed in a mirror and what that does to the hour hand.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
